sources.news_title: UK PM: IRGC 'almost certainly' behind RAF Fairford terror plot
sources.text:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that intelligence assessments indicate Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was almost certainly responsible for directing a suspected terrorist plot targeting RAF Fairford, a British air base previously used by American bombers for strikes against Iran.
Addressing parliament, Burnham said British authorities believe the operation was organized from Iranian territory.
“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told lawmakers, as quoted by the Reuters news agency.
The suspected plot prompted a major security operation near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England, where five British men were arrested in the early hours of September 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives-related offenses.
American officials previously told Reuters that investigators suspected an Iranian-linked plan to attack the base using drones.
Last week, US President Donald Trump said a threat connected to Iran had led Washington to withdraw its bombers from RAF Fairford.
Iran has denied involvement in the incident and challenged Britain to produce evidence supporting its accusations.
“Tehran has had no involvement in this matter, and if the British government possesses any documents or evidence to support its claims, it should present them," Iranian Ambassador to Britain Seyed Ali Mousavi said, according to the Iranian state news agency IRNA.
Although British officials have publicly attributed the suspected operation to Iran, several details of the investigation remain unresolved.
The five men initially detained were subsequently released without charge on police bail “under stringent conditions". Two additional suspects, including a British-Iranian national, were also released.
Investigators reported finding petrol in vans seized during the operation but said no viable explosive devices had been discovered.
Burnham pledged to take additional measures against Iranian-backed networks operating in Britain.
“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. “We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm."

sources.news_title: UK’s Burnham says Iran’s IRGC likely behind airbase incident
sources.text:
LONDON - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford airbase in Britain was “highly likely” to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The RAF Fairford base in southwest England, which had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, became the focal point for a major security response after five British men were arrested nearby in the early hours of September 27 on suspected terrorism and explosive offenses.
US officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack, and last week US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted a decision to withdraw the bombers from the base.
“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC),” Burnham told parliament. Tehran has rejected any suggestion it was involved in the Fairford incident, saying it amounted to “unfounded and malicious speculations.” Details around the suspected plot remain thin. The five detained men were later released without charge on police bail “under stringent conditions,” and two other arrested men, including a British-Iranian national, have also been released. Detectives have said gasoline but no viable explosive had been found in vans seized along with the five men. However, both police and Burnham have pointed toward the involvement of a foreign state. “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil,” Burnham said. “We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.” Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries, including the UK, US, Canada, France, and Germany, issued a statement condemning “Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyberattacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners.” “The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors,” the statement said.
The statement noted that the RAF Fairford plot comes after a “campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists, and US interests.”
It stressed that any Iranian attempt to “threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable.” Tehran, the foreign ministries said, “should be in no doubt that we are united and remain committed to safeguarding our sovereignty and strengthening our international coordination, bolstering our national resilience, protecting our communities, and ensuring that those responsible are held to account.”
The statement was also signed by Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden.

sources.news_title: British Airbase Plot ‘Almost Certainly Directed’ by Iran Guards, Says UK PM
sources.text:
Britain's government Monday accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of being behind a major scare at a UK airbase used by the United States, as allies including Washington warned Tehran against hostile acts.
Iran denied any involvement.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the British parliament that Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) "almost certainly directed" an incident at the Royal Air Force base of Fairford in southwest England last month.
The US, which had been using the base for its war in Iran, abruptly withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the site last week after the mysterious episode on September 27.
Burnham said Britain's assessment of the incident was that it "is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard".
"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams," he told MPs.
Iran's state news agency IRNA reported that "the Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base" and "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
Shortly after Burnham spoke to parliament, 29 countries, including the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France and Germany, released a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks".
The statement said such attacks included "acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners".
"Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," it read.
The Foreign Office confirmed in its own statement Monday that Iran's ambassador to the UK had been summoned for talks.
"We are also announcing the designation of two Iranian nationals for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," foreign minister Ed Miliband said.
The foreign ministry said the individuals included Ruhollah Bazghandi, the IRGC's head of counterespionage operations, who is "now subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification".
Speculation has swirled about the incident since police were called to the base after a local farmer reported a group of men with several white vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.
- 'Major' incident -
Despite a major counter-terrorism probe, seven suspects arrested in the days following, including a British-Iranian national, have all since been released on bail. None has been charged.
The incident was declared "major" by British authorities and triggered the evacuation of a nearby village.
But the source and nature of the threat have remained shrouded in mystery.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but did recover some petrol, according to officials.
Burnham has previously said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, which Tehran has rejected.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and US bombers and other planes had been seen taking off and landing at the base.
US President Donald Trump has said Washington withdrew its bombers because of "threats" he believed were linked to Tehran.
In the foreign ministry statement, Miliband noted that the UK had already "designated the IRGC under our new state threats powers, and imposed major sanctions on those responsible for Iran's malign activity".

sources.text: By — Sylvia Hui, Associated Press Sylvia Hui, Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/suspected-plot-at-u-s-run-air-base-almost-certainly-directed-by-iran-uk-prime-minister-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Suspected plot at U.S.-run air base almost certainly directed by Iran, UK prime minister says World Oct 12, 2026 6:25 PM EDT LONDON (AP) — A suspected plot to attack a U.S.-run military air base in England was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday. Burnham previously said there are strong indications Iran was linked to the apparent plan last month to attack the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran in the ongoing war. Police have arrested seven men in the investigation into the alleged plot, but all suspects have been released on bail and no one has been charged so far. Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told lawmakers. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil." Police found gasoline but no explosives in the suspects' vehicles Scores of residents near the air base were evacuated from their homes on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the initial five suspects who were arrested on the scene, but no explosives. All the suspects arrested are in their 20s. None has been identified, though police said six are British nationals while one is a dual U.K.-Iranian citizen. On Monday, the British government summoned the Iranian ambassador, who reiterated that Tehran was not involved in the suspected plot and urged the U.K. to provide evidence supporting its claims. The U.K. also said it added two Iranians, including the head of counterespionage operations in the Revolutionary Guard, to its sanctions list. Authorities said the two were involved in conducting espionage and attacks on behalf of Iran's government in Europe and the U.S. The U.S. pulled its bombers last week from RAF Fairford, about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, and the aircraft have now been redeployed to their home bases, the Pentagon said. The Trump administration has said it believed the base faced Iranian threats intended to kill as many American troops and destroy as many U.S. planes as possible. The British government allowed the U.S. military to use RAF Fairford for what it called defensive strikes on Iranian missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on U.K. interests and Britain's allies in the Gulf. U.S. joins many Western countries in condemning Iranian proxy attacks Officials have said that local proxies linked to Iran were behind a string of arson and other attacks on the U.S., Britain and other countries, many of them targeting Jewish communities and intended to sow fear. British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months to December 2025. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said Monday that the Fairford air base incident "speaks to a wider trend." "States like Iran are using proxies to conduct hostile activity here in Britain. They pay criminals or exploit naive volunteers, attacking our country and its citizens while maintaining an air of plausible deniability," she said. In a joint statement released Monday, the foreign ministers of the U.K., U.S. and about two dozen Western countries condemned Iranian attacks on their territory. They said the Fairford incident demonstrated Iran's "continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors." "Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts," the statement said. sources.news_title: Terror Plot at UK Airbase ‘Almost Certainly’ Directed by Iran, British PM Says
sources.text:
Last month’s suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford, an airbase shared with the United States in England, was likely coordinated and directed by Iran’s ruling regime, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Oct. 12.
“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran—almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard [IRGC],” Burnham told lawmakers.
Burnham said investigators were in close contact with the United States about protective security at shared military bases in the UK and were continuing to investigate the case.
Seven suspects, all in their 20s, were arrested on terror and explosives charges for their alleged involvement in the RAF Fairford incident on Sept. 27.
Police responded to local tips about suspicious activity near the facility in Gloucestershire, England. Officers stopped three vans heading toward the airbase used by American forces to launch strikes against Iran.
The Pentagon has since removed its heavy bombers from the base. The men have been released from custody and have not been formally charged.
In another incident, two Latvian men were arrested on espionage charges on Oct. 7 after they allegedly broke into the RAF Molesworth airbase, used by U.S. and NATO intelligence teams, near London.
Burnham didn’t say whether the two airbase incidents were linked, but he vowed to investigate any future threats from Iran.
“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil,” Burnham said. “We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams. And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.”
The United States and the UK joined 27 other countries to “condemn in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities” against the countries and their partners.
“We recognize the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September,” the countries said in a joint statement after Burnham’s announcement. “The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors.”
The nations vowed to “investigate, disrupt, and prosecute” all attempts to “silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people through proxies or other means.”
“Iran should be in no doubt that we are united and remain committed to safeguarding our sovereignty and strengthening our international coordination, bolstering our national resilience, protecting our communities, and ensuring that those responsible are held to account,” the countries stated.
The alleged attempted terror attack comes after recent attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists, and U.S. interests. The pro-Iranian Islamist group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI) claimed to have instigated the attacks, according to state officials.
The incidents included a March 9 attack using a homemade explosive at a synagogue in Liège, Belgium; attacks against Jewish institutions in the Netherlands targeting a synagogue on March 13, 14, and 15; and a foiled bomb plot against a Bank of America branch in Paris on March 28.
The United States and other countries called for the HAYI attacks to end earlier this month, saying the relationship between Iranian security services and international and local criminal groups was long-standing.
“Attempts to kill, kidnap, harass, intimidate, or otherwise attack people on our soil, [undermine] national sovereignty and international norms. These actions must stop immediately,” the countries stated on Oct. 6.

sources.text:
UK premier says Iran ‘almost certainly’ directed UK air base plot, announces sanctions
Iran denied involvement in the Fairford air base incident, urging Britain to provide evidence for its allegations
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that last month’s alleged terror plot targeting a British air base was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as he announced fresh sanctions against two Iranian men.
However, Iran on Monday denied any involvement in an incident at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase, which has been used by the United States in its war with the Islamic republic.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any".
Addressing Parliament, Burnham said the UK assessment was that the alleged plot, which led to five arrests on suspicion of terror offenses, was highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran.
“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” he told MPs.
“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams.
“And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.”
In late September, a major security incident occurred at RAF Fairford, a Gloucestershire airbase used by the US Air Force. The incident triggered a large-scale counter-terrorism investigation.
Separately, the UK government also announced that it summoned Iran’s ambassador for ongoing "malign activity."
Read More: US removes B-1 bombers from UK base amid security concerns
“Iran’s continued attempts to undermine the security of the United Kingdom and international partners through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable," Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement.
"This Government will never waiver in our commitment to tacking Iran’s unacceptable actions and protecting our national security. We have already designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) under our new state threats powers," he added.
Britain has also imposed sanctions on two Iranian men, including an asset freeze and a ban on entering the UK.
'We stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis'
Burnham also addressed the escalating situation involving Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, saying he had discussed the issue with US President Donald Trump last month on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
“In my meeting with President Trump, we discussed the situation in the Middle East. I confirmed Britain's decision to send air defense and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refueling support," he said.
"I can confirm today it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International Airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis,” he added.
No reopening 2016 Brexit referendum
Burnham also ruled out reopening the Brexit referendum or revising his government's manifesto commitments on relations with the EU, while advocating closer cooperation with the bloc to boost economic growth and address migration.
He also said he respected the result of the 2016 referendum, in which Britain voted to leave the EU, but argued that pragmatic cooperation with European partners could serve the country's interests.
"I am not reopening the referendum. I respect the referendum result," he said.
Also Read: UK examines foreign state involvement in airbase plot
Burnham said his government would pursue opportunities to strengthen the British economy and improve cooperation to tackle migrant boat crossings in the English Channel.
"The deal that I've inherited coming into office represents an opportunity to secure progress on both of those things," he said, adding that rejecting such opportunities would be "a dereliction of duty from any member of this House," he noted.
‘It’s a conversation we must have’
Ahead of next month's UK-EU summit, Burnham called for discussions on the future relationship between Britain and the bloc, saying closer ties could help promote growth, control migration, and strengthen security.
"If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling migration, upholding our values and our security, it is a conversation we must have," he said.
However, Burnham ruled out rejoining the EU single market or customs union or restoring freedom of movement, citing commitments in Labour's 2024 general election manifesto.
Mentioning what he “can’t do” to improve growth in the UK, he said: “I also want to maintain trust in politics. And I'm afraid I'm not prepared to revisit the red lines in our manifesto.”
The manifesto pledged to keep Britain outside the EU while seeking to reset relations and deepen ties with European partners.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of attempting to distract the public by raising claims of Russian interference in the 2016 referendum.
She questioned whether he considered the referendum result legitimate and called on Burnham to publish evidence if he believes Russia influenced the outcome.
"This is lazy thinking from people who don't have solutions to the real problems we face," Badenoch said.
But Burnham accused the Conservatives of being "in denial about, and not open to seeing, how we can move forward to a better position for the country."
He said public opinion in Britain has shifted in favor of a different approach to relations with the EU, while insisting that his government would respect its existing commitments.

UK: Iran 'highly likely' to be behind RAF Fairford incident
October 12, 2026
The British government has accused Iran of involvement in a security alert outside a UK/US airbase in southern England last month, summoning the ambassador and announcing sanctions against two individuals.
Five British nationals were arrested in the vicinity of the RAF Fairford airbase on September 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses. They were later released on bail under strict conditions, and another arrest followed days later.
Police had already said they were considering the possibility of a foreign state actor's involvement, not least given RAF Fairford's importance to the US Air Force as one of the European bases that handles heavy bombers like B-1's and B-52's, with ample range to reach Iran.
What did Prime Minister Andy Burnham tell parliament?
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in the House of Commons on Monday that the UK might yet put further sanctions on Iran in response.
He said there were indications of Iran coordinating the potential plot.
"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," he said. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil."
The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited.
Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the vans. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum.
"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said.
Foreign Secretary Miliband says Iranian ambassador summoned
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil."
Iran's state news agency IRNA reported Ambassador Ali Moussavi as "categorically rejecting the accusations" and calling on the British government "to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
Miliband said that two individuals would be subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification.
He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network.
Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas."
Joint statement from 29 countries condemns 'Iran's use of violent attacks'
Shortly afterwards, a total of 29 countries issued a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks."
It said these included "the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
All of the so-called "Five Eyes" alliance and most European NATO members were listed among the signatories, including but not limited to the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Spain and Ireland.
In the aftermath of the September 27 incident at Fairford, the high-tech US B-1 bombers left the airbase. The older and larger contingent of B-52's remained there.
RAF Fairford is one of several airbases in southern England with a large US usage footprint. It's located around two hours' drive west of London, in a rural area north of Swindon.
As with most such bases, it can trace its roots back to the second World War when Nazi Germany occupied most of mainland Europe and Allied powers were operating air raids and preparing for the D-Day landings out of Britain.

“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” said Burnham.
The prime minister vowed to “crack down” on Iran, despite the UK’s slightly hesitant approach in America’s Operation Epic Fury.
“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm,” the prime minister added.
Iran has denied any involvement in the alleged plot.
Despite multiple arrests in the foiled terror plot, a handful of suspects were released on bail, leading to Trump criticizing UK officials for the move, saying he was surprised by the move and “wouldn’t have done that.”
UK authorities have been guarded in releasing too many details about the suspects, but confirmed that those initially arrested were all UK nationals living in London and in their 20s.
Since the incident, the U.S. relocated the bombers from RAF Fairford, with Trump pointing to security concerns over the base.
Despite the latest developments, Trump maintains that Iranian officials want to make a deal; however, the president remains open to more military strikes but continues to believe the conflict with Iran will be “over soon.”

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of almost certainly directing a suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford, which is a British air base used by US bombers during military operations against Iran. The accusation is a big escalation in tensions between London and Tehran, with the UK government threatening further sanctions against Iran and its powerful security force.
Addressing Parliament on Monday, Burnham said British authorities believed the suspected operation had been coordinated from Iran. The incident triggered a major security response after five British men were arrested near the base in southwest England on September 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offences.
"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told Parliament.
RAF FAIRFORD IN SPOTLIGHT
RAF Fairford, located in Gloucestershire in southwest England, is a British military base used by the US Air Force. It became a focus of security concerns after being used by American bombers to carry out strikes on Iran during the conflict in the Middle East. US officials told news agency Reuters that investigators were examining a suspected plot involving a possible drone attack on the base. US President Donald Trump also said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the withdrawal of bombers from the facility.
The security alert has raised concerns about the vulnerability of military installations supporting operations against Iran, even when they are located outside the immediate conflict zone.
The arrests took place after suspicious activity was reported near the base. Police found petrol in vans associated with the five men, but no viable explosives were discovered, according to reports. The suspects were subsequently released on police bail under strict conditions.
Two other men were also arrested in connection with the investigation, including a British-Iranian national. They too have been released, while inquiries into the suspected plot continue. No charges have been confirmed in the case.
IRAN DEMANDS EVIDENCE
Tehran has strongly rejected Britain's accusations, arguing that the government should provide evidence rather than publicly attribute responsibility to Iran. Iran's Ambassador to Britain, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said, according to Iran's state news agency IRNA: "Tehran has had no involvement in this matter, and if the British government possesses any documents or evidence to support its claims, it should present them,"

The British government has previously accused Iran of using criminal networks and intermediaries to pursue threats against individuals in the UK, including alleged assassination and kidnapping plots. Tehran has repeatedly denied such accusations.

WESTERN ALLIES CONDEMN IRANIAN ACTIVITIES
The allegations have also drawn a response from Britain's international allies. Foreign ministries from 29 countries, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States, condemned what they described as Iran's use of violent attacks, including alleged lethal plots, arson, sabotage and cyberattacks.

The latest developments add to tensions between Iran and Western governments following the conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel.

sources.text:
For decades since the end of the Second World War, Britain’s “special relationship” with the United States rested on more than shared history and diplomatic rhetoric. Britain provided bases, intelligence, nuclear cooperation, warships, soldiers, and, perhaps most importantly, a government Washington could generally expect to stand beside it during a crisis. But the recent departure of 12 American B-1B Lancer bombers from RAF Fairford following security threats against the base raises an uncomfortable question: Can the United States still rely upon Britain as a serious military ally?

The bombers had been deployed to RAF Fairford, the strategically important Royal Air Force base routinely used by the United States for bomber operations in Europe. Following the arrest of several suspects in connection with suspicious activity around the base, and intelligence concerning a potential Iranian-linked drone attack, the entire deployed B-1 force left Britain. President Donald J. Trump subsequently acknowledged that threats played a role in moving the aircraft.
The Fairford Debacle.
Five British men were initially arrested following suspicious activity involving vehicles near the base. They were subsequently released on bail just a day later. A British-Iranian dual national was later arrested and bailed; additional arrests followed.
From Washington’s perspective, the more important question is whether Britain can adequately secure a base housing billions of dollars’ worth of American strategic aircraft against the sort of comparatively cheap drone threat that has transformed modern warfare in places like Ukraine and the Middle East.
Trump himself expressed surprise over the release of suspects, while the B-1s ultimately departed. Whatever conclusions the investigation eventually produces, the sequence of events hardly inspires confidence. Fairford, however, is merely the latest example of a much wider problem.
Chagos and the Limits of the Special Relationship.
Britain’s handling of the Chagos Islands has already raised similar questions over whether Washington can automatically rely upon access to British territory during wartime. Diego Garcia, the largest island in the Chagos Archipelago, is one of America’s most strategically important overseas military facilities. Sitting in the middle of the Indian Ocean, it provides America with a vital staging point for operations stretching from the Middle East to Asia.
London, under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, pursued a controversial agreement to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, which has a close relationship to China, while retaining arrangements intended to preserve the Anglo-American base on Diego Garcia in exchange for substantial cash payments.
The problem became especially visible during the Iran conflict. Britain did not completely prohibit American use of British bases. The British government authorized narrowly defined American operations involving British territory. But the Labour government continued to insist that the use of British bases for combat operations was subject to approval on a case-by-case basis.
The question facing the Trump administration is not simply whether Britain technically remains an ally, but whether American commanders can confidently assume access to strategically vital British facilities during a rapidly developing conflict.
The National Pulse keeps you informed about international developments that affect American security. If you value the work of Raheem J. Kassam and his team, please JOIN THE NATIONAL PULSE or MAKE A DONATION today.
Britain’s Vanishing Royal Navy.
Britain is an island nation dependent upon international trade and maritime freedom, making the security of waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz a direct British national interest. However, when tensions escalated in the Gulf, the British government did little to provide any sort of armed response.
Asked in Parliament about deploying forces to Hormuz, the government said it was considering military options while declining to discuss operational planning. The reality is that Britain’s political hesitation coincides with an increasingly severe shortage of available warships. Official Ministry of Defence statistics showed Britain with just 52 Royal Navy surface vessels as of April 2026, following years of contraction and the retirement of additional frigates and amphibious ships, down from 1,176 navy vessels following the Second World War. The Ministry of Defence maintains that the Navy retains high operational readiness, but it has declined to publish precisely how many warships are immediately available for operations, making it unclear how many ships Britain’s navy could send to a theater like the Strait of Hormuz even if it wanted to.
An Army Struggling with Recruitment.
Britain’s Army is faring no better and has undergone a similar decline. According to House of Commons Library figures, the British Army had approximately 70,759 trade-trained regular personnel in April 2026, below its target strength of 73,000. Across the armed forces, Britain was approximately 8,460 trained personnel below target. The Royal Navy and Royal Marines were around seven percent below target, while the Royal Air Force was roughly 12 percent short.
By contrast, Britain had approximately 186,000 full-time armed forces personnel in 2012. By 2026, that number had fallen to roughly 149,000, a reduction of around 37,000 personnel in little more than a decade. Britain’s Army is now smaller than at any point after 1793, just before the Napoleonic wars, according to some estimates.
Despite this, Britain continues to talk like the global military power it was in prior decades, while maintaining armed forces increasingly lacking the manpower and numerical depth traditionally required of one.
From America’s Closest Ally to Strategic Liability?
Britain remains deeply integrated into American defense and intelligence structures. Five Eyes intelligence cooperation, nuclear collaboration, NATO planning, joint special forces operations, and America’s continued access to British facilities still give Britain a privileged position among America’s allies.
For much of the last century, Britain offered Washington a uniquely useful combination: geography, intelligence, military capability, diplomatic support, and governments prepared to fight alongside America from Korea and the Persian Gulf to Afghanistan and Iraq. That is why the image of America’s B-1 bombers departing RAF Fairford is so striking.
American bombers arrived in Britain because Britain was supposed to provide a secure forward operating location from which the United States could project military power to places such as Iran, something Britain seemingly cannot do itself.
The danger for the special relationship is that Washington may increasingly find itself asking a very different question: not whether Britain remains America’s friend, but whether Britain can be relied on.

sources.text:
Time to round up all Iranian terror suspects
The suspected terror incident at the RAF’s Fairford base in south western England has raised alarming questions as to how the UK should deal with any future potential Iranian threats.
Perhaps the time has finally come for the Labour administration at Westminster to forget its snowflake attitude towards Iran and throw its weight 100 per cent politically and militarily behind Donald Trump’s campaign against Iran.
Put bluntly, is Downing Street going to wait until suspected Iranian terrorists carry out either a suicide bombing or even unleash an Omagh-style no-warning massacre before it gives the green light to the round-up of terror suspects?
Because The United States was specifically using RAF Fairford as a base for American bombers to attack Iran, the militant Islamic regime in Iran in turn has threatened to carry out attacks in the UK.
Warfare now in the 21st century is roughly divided into three main types. Firstly, nuclear warfare, which would be devastating for the globe as a whole as no one seriously wants to press the red buttons.
Secondly, conventional warfare, which is more commonly known as ‘boots on the ground’ as witnessed by both the old Soviet Union and the Allied Coalition in Afghanistan.
Thirdly, hybrid warfare, which blurs the lines between actual conflict and what is seen as a peace process. Again, put bluntly, this is just a fancy term for good, old fashioned terrorism.
This could also include cyber terrorism and security alerts which disrupt civilian life. Iran certainly would not dare the first type - nuclear, although could terrorists be capable of setting off a so-called ‘dirty bomb’ or is that the stuff of Hollywood film fiction?
Secondly, obviously given the geographical distance between the United Kingdom and Iran, there would be no way actual Iranian Revolutionary Guards would indulge in a uniformed attack in the UK.
This leaves the more obvious method - hybrid, or terrorism, as witnessed with the incident at the RAF base. The real danger is that a cell of radicalised terrorists now exists in mainland Britain, seeking to carry out - as Trump put its - ‘serious damage’ to several potential military, political or civilian targets in mainland Britain.
As well as a suicide bomber cell, there is also the threat posed by a so-called ‘lone wolf’ terrorist along the lines of the Far Right activist Anders Brevik who killed 77 people in bomb and gun attacks in Norway in July 2011.
The key question which must be answered by the British intelligence community is - how do potential terrorists enter the UK?
Are we talking about so-called ‘sleeper’ cells that have been in the country for months, even years, before they are activated, or have they sneaked into the UK under the cover of the small boat crisis which has seen thousands of illegal asylum seekers and migrants cross the English Channel from France in recent years.
British PM Andy Burnham has already publicly recognised the potential threat from Iran because of the UK allowing the US to use English bases. But he still has to clearly address the issue of what the UK can realistically do to combat any terrorist threat from Iran.
A starting point can be to radically slash the foreign aid budget and divert that money into boosting the intelligence services and especially surveillance of potential terrorists either already in the UK or planning to enter the UK.
Given the number of illegal migrants who have already entered the UK, perhaps a more radical solution is needed, namely the introduction of the controversial method of selective internment.
However, the scheme does not have a good reputation as when it was introduced in Northern Ireland during the early Troubles in the Seventies, it was based on false or outdated information and only served to boost the IRA, not hinder it.
Hopefully, given the advances in intelligence gathering since that 1970s fiasco, potential suspects can be rounded up and held in the British equivalent of the former American base - Camp X Ray - at Guantanamo Bay.
From an intelligence point of view, the British and US authorities need to determine if the RAF Fairford incident could be firm evidence of Iran developing a so-called Triple Alliance of Terror. Iran already supports Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza. Could the third part be a similar IRA-style movement in the UK?
Could the purpose of any potential terror campaign in the UK be Iran trying to drive a political wedge between Westminster and the White House? If Iran is too skeptical about attacking the US directly in retaliation for American air strikes on Iran, Plan B would be to launch terrorist attacks against those nations which either allow the US to use its air bases, or allow US bombers to enter their air space en route to bombing targets in Iran?
The situation which the UK specifically and NATO in general finds itself in is that since the end of the formal Cold War with the old communist Soviet Union, there has been a ‘dumbing down’ of the British security forces in terms of training, human and physical resources, and especially budget cuts.
Has this in turn fuelled the development of hybrid war whereby the so-called nuclear super powers get ‘puppet’ organisations in other nations to do their work for them? Put bluntly, any Iranian activity in the UK would be met with quiet support in the other Triple Alliance of Russia, China and North Korea.
In this case, we could see the UK sucked into a so-called proxy war by the back door by having to combat Iranian terror alerts on UK territory, thus diverting much-needed aid from Ukraine and NATO.
In this respect, potential Iranian terror cells would be copying the terror campaign of the Provisional IRA’s so-called ‘England Department’ which targeted places, people and the security forces in mainland Britain during the Troubles.

Washington, Oct 12 (SocialNews.XYZ) The United States and 28 other governments have condemned the Iranian hostile activities as they backed Britain’s allegations that Iran was involved in an attempted terrorist attack at RAF Fairford.
The joint statement, released by the US State Department on Monday, linked the September 27 incident to broader concerns about attacks targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and American interests in Europe.

“We recognize the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September,” the statement said.
The diplomatic response brings together the United States, Canada, Britain, Australia, New Zealand and a broad group of European governments.
The signatories condemned activities they attributed to Iran, including lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyberattacks and other operations against their countries and partners.
They said attempts to threaten, intimidate, silence, harass, harm or coerce people on their territories were unacceptable, whether conducted through proxies or by other means.
The warning extended to anyone carrying out hostile activities on behalf of Iran or another state. The governments pledged to identify, investigate, disrupt and prosecute such acts.
They also committed to strengthening international coordination, protecting communities, safeguarding sovereignty and holding those responsible to account.
The statement attributed the assessment of Iranian involvement at Fairford to Britain.
The governments referred separately to a recent campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and US interests. They said those attacks had been claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, identified in the statement by the acronym HAYI.

sources.text:
Andy Burnham has warned that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was “almost certainly” behind a suspected terror plot targeting RAF Fairford, escalating tensions between London and Tehran as questions grow over the security of US military assets stationed in Britain.
The Prime Minister told MPs that the Government assessed it was “highly likely” the alleged operation had been coordinated in Iran, raising the prospect of fresh sanctions against Tehran and a tougher crackdown on suspected Iranian-backed criminal networks operating on British soil.
“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” Burnham said in the Commons.
“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil.”
He added that the Government would use its “full range of powers” to target Iranian-linked networks and their financial resources, alongside further sanctions intended to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to threaten British interests.
The Iranian ambassador to the UK has been summoned, the Foreign Minister confirmed, as the diplomatic fallout from the suspected plot intensifies.
The allegations follow the arrest last week of five British men on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, a strategically important airbase used by the US Air Force as a staging point for long-range bomber operations in Europe.
The arrests have raised fresh concerns over the potential reach of Iranian intelligence and its alleged use of criminal networks to threaten Western military installations. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have previously described the base as a legitimate target.
US President Donald Trump said last week that a threat linked to Iran had prompted American B-1 bombers to be moved from the base. The aircraft had recently been used in US strikes on Iran.
“We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there? It costs very little money to move them,” Trump told reporters on Monday.
“So we had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we just move them, and that sort of alleviates that. And we actually know the people that made the threat.”
Asked whether those behind the threat were linked to Iran, Trump replied: “They would be linked to Iran.”
Vice-President JD Vance also said Washington believed Tehran continued to pose a serious security threat, describing the relocation of the bombers as a precautionary measure.
“We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they’re trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engaged in acts of terrorism against the United States (and others), so we are being extremely cautious, and that’s all I’d say about that,” Vance told reporters.
However, the US administration has offered differing explanations for the aircraft’s sudden departure. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the suspected Iranian plot and the movement of the bombers, adding that the Pentagon was “constantly reallocating resources where they need to be”.
A Nato military source nevertheless warned that “it is still believed that Iran poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK”.
Significant questions remain unanswered about the arrests, the precise nature of the suspected plot and the evidence underpinning the allegations of Iranian direction.
Tehran has rejected accusations of involvement, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi dismissing the claims as baseless.
Writing on X, Araqchi said: “I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You’re barking up the wrong tree.”
The dispute now presents Britain with a delicate security and diplomatic challenge: responding to what Burnham describes as a potentially state-directed threat while establishing the facts behind an investigation that remains incomplete.
Any further sanctions would add to pressure on Tehran at a time of heightened confrontation between Iran and the US, while the presence of American bomber aircraft at British bases continues to place the UK close to the centre of the wider conflict.
For now, the Government has made its assessment clear. But with Iran denying responsibility and Washington offering differing accounts of the bombers’ relocation, the evidence behind the suspected plot will be central to determining the next steps.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the British parliament that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) “almost certainly directed” an incident at Royal Air Force Fairford in southwest England last month.
The US, which had been using the base for its war in Iran, abruptly withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the site last week after the mysterious episode on September 27.
Burnham said Britain’s assessment of the incident was that it “is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard”.
“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams,” he told MPs.
Shortly afterwards, 29 countries, including the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France and Germany, released a joint statement denouncing “in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks”.
The statement said such attacks included “acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners”.
“Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable,” it read.
The Foreign Office confirmed in its own statement Monday that Iran’s ambassador to the UK had been summoned for talks.
“We are also announcing the designation of two Iranian nationals for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas,” foreign minister Ed Miliband said.
The foreign ministry said the individuals included Ruhollah Bazghandi, the IRGC’s head of counterespionage operations, who is “now subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification”.
Speculation has swirled about the incident since police were called to the base after a local farmer reported a group of men with several white vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.
‘Major’ incident
Despite a major counter-terrorism probe, seven suspects arrested in the days following, including a British-Iranian national, have all since been released on bail. None has been charged.
The incident was declared “major” by British authorities and triggered the evacuation of a nearby village.
But the source and nature of the threat have remained shrouded in mystery.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but did recover some petrol, according to officials.
Burnham has previously said there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, which Tehran has rejected.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for “specific defensive operations into Iran,” and US bombers and other planes had been seen taking off and landing at the base.
US President Donald Trump has said Washington withdrew its bombers because of “threats” he believed were linked to Tehran.
In the foreign ministry statement, Miliband noted that the UK had already “designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) under our new state threats powers, and imposed major sanctions on those responsible for Iran’s malign activity”.
